docs.title: Providing intel on cybersecurity risks across African continent and third world countries
docs.text:
Welcome to NetIris, your overview of everything cybersecurity.

As digital adoption grows, especially in mobile money and social media, cyber risks aren't left behind. NetIris provides plain-language guides and aggregated threat data to help you understand these threats and protect yourself.

docs.title: How can we help?
docs.text:
Read plain-language guides on how to spot scams, secure your mobile money, and protect your accounts. No technical jargon.

  • Go to the Wiki

Explore the threat dashboard and recent security data.

  • Open the Dashboard

Learn about network security and download our educational command-line scanner to test your own systems safely.

  • Learn about the scanner

docs.title: Why NetIris?
docs.text:
Cybersecurity information is often for large corporations or advanced professionals or advanced IT professionals. NetIris bridges that gap.

  • For Students and Teachers: Understand the digital risks you face daily on campus and online.

  • For Small Businesses: Protect your mobile money, customer data, and digital presence from fraud.

  • For Journalists And Researchers: Access verified, cited data on the cyber threat landscape in Africa and Third World Countries.

Project status:Public Beta

Netiris is in its Release 1(Public Beta) phase. The site is actively under development.

docs.title: About NetIris
docs.text:
NetIris is a student-led, non-commercial cybersecurity awareness project focused on Africa.

Our goal is to bridge the gap between complex cyber threat data and the people who need it most: students, small business owners, teachers, and everyday mobile money users. We provide plain-language guides and aggregated threat data to help you understand digital risks and protect yourself.

Non-Commercial Project NetIris is strictly an educational and portfolio project. We do not sell services, show advertisements, offer paid consultations, or accept sponsorships. If you see "NetIris" associated with a paid service or commercial consultancy, it is not affiliated with this website.

NetIris is part of an ongoing effort to build practical experience in data engineering, web development, and cybersecurity research.

docs.title: How to get in touch
docs.text:
We welcome feedback, corrections, and suggestions for new wiki articles.

  • Report an error or suggest an article: Open an issue on our GitHub Repository.
  • General feedback: Email us

Note: We are a small, independent project. Please allow a few days for a response.

docs.title: 1. Communications Authority of Kenya (National KE-CIRT/CC)
docs.text:
• Source Name: Communications Authority of Kenya (CA) / National KE-CIRT/CC
  • Report Title: Cyber Security Report Q1 2026-2027
  • Link
  • Date Checked: November 2, 2026
  • License/Attribution: Public government report; requires attribution to the Communications Authority of Kenya.
  • Key Findings: Detected national cyber threat events rose by 14.45% in a single quarter (July–September 2026) to reach 2.696 billion. Social engineering, stolen credentials, and malicious links targeting mobile ecosystems drove a 34.43% surge in issued mobile threat advisories.

docs.title: 2. INTERPOL African Cyberthreat Assessment Report
docs.text:
• Source Name: INTERPOL Africa Cybercrime Operations Desk
  • Report Title: African Cyberthreat Assessment Report 2026
  • Link
  • Date Checked: November 2, 2026
  • License/Attribution: Publicly available report; requires clear attribution to INTERPOL.
  • Key Findings: Generative AI tools are actively enabling up to 55% of all cybercrime across Africa. Social engineering, smishing (SMS phishing), and synthetic identity fraud are specifically targeting mobile financial services and public sector institutions.

docs.title: Privacy Policy
docs.text:
Last updated: November 2026

NetIris is built with privacy in mind. This page explains plainly what information is collected when you visit this website.

docs.title: What we do NOT collect
docs.text:
• No Cookies: We do not use tracking cookies, advertising cookies, or session cookies.
  • No Accounts: You do not need to sign up, log in, or provide an email address to read our articles or view the dashboard.
  • No Analytics: We do not use third-party analytics tools (like Google Analytics) to track your behavior, clicks, or location.

docs.title: What our hosting provider collects
docs.text:
NetIris is hosted on GitHub Pages. Like all web hosts, GitHub automatically processes standard web server logs to keep the site running and secure.

When you visit the site, GitHub's servers may temporarily log standard technical information, such as:

  • Your IP address (anonymized or kept briefly for security)
  • The type of browser and device you are using
  • The time and date of your visit
  • The pages you requested

This data is processed by GitHub according to their own privacy policies. NetIris does not have access to this raw log data, nor do we use it to identify individual visitors. For more details, please read GitHub's Privacy Statement.

docs.title: Dashboard Data Privacy
docs.text:
The threat data shown on our Dashboard is strictly aggregated.

  • We never publish raw IP addresses, URLs, or file hashes.
  • We never publish data that can identify a specific individual or a specific victim's device.
  • If a specific country or category has very few recorded events, we mark it as "low count" to prevent anyone from being identified through the data.

docs.title: Changes to this policy
docs.text: Because this is a student project in active development, this privacy policy may be updated as we add new features. Any significant changes will be posted on this page with an updated date.

docs.title: Understanding Smishing and Mobile Money Fraud
Understanding Smishing and Mobile Money Fraud
docs.text: Mobile money is a vital part of daily life across Africa. However, its rapid adoption has made it a primary target for cybercriminals. According to INTERPOL's 2026 African Cyberthreat Assessment Report, generative AI tools are now enabling up to 55% of all cybercrime across the continent. A significant portion of this activity involves smishing (SMS phishing) and synthetic identity fraud specifically targeting mobile financial services.

docs.title: How These Scams Work
docs.text: Criminals use AI to create highly convincing, personalized text messages that mimic official alerts from banks or mobile network operators. They often create a false sense of urgency, claiming your account is locked, a transaction failed, or you must verify your identity immediately.

docs.title: What to do: Protect your mobile money
docs.text:
• Never share your PIN or OTP: Legitimate organizations will never ask for your Personal Identification Number (PIN) or One-Time Password (OTP) via SMS or phone call.
  • Verify independently: If you receive an urgent message, do not click any links. Open your mobile money app directly or call the official customer service number found on the back of your SIM card or the provider's official website.
  • Report suspicious activity: Forward suspicious SMS messages to your mobile network provider's fraud hotline and report the incident to your national CERT (e.g., KE-CIRT/CC in Kenya)
